module_title: Introduction to PVC Pipes and Plumbing Systems

lessons.title: Identifying Common PVC Pipe Sizes Used in African Homes (20mm to 110mm)
lessons.body: In African homes, PVC pipes come in standard metric sizes measured by outside diameter (OD). The most common sizes you will see are 20mm, 25mm, 32mm, 40mm, 50mm, 63mm, 75mm, 90mm, and 110mm. These are used for different purposes: 20mm and 25mm are for small supply lines to taps and toilets; 32mm and 40mm are for sink and basin waste; 50mm and 63mm are for shower and bath drains; 75mm and 90mm are for main soil stacks; and 110mm is for underground sewer lines and toilet outlets. In many markets, pipes are sold in 4-meter or 6-meter lengths. You can identify the size by looking at the markings printed on the pipe: it will say something like 'PVC 110mm x 4m' or 'uPVC 32mm'. If the markings are worn off, use a measuring tape to measure the outside diameter. For example, a 110mm pipe will measure about 110mm across the outside. Be careful: some older pipes use imperial sizes like 1/2 inch or 2 inch. A 1/2 inch pipe is about 21mm, which is close to 20mm but not exactly the same. Always match the pipe size to the fittings you have. If you are replacing a section, take a small piece of the old pipe to the shop to compare. In rural areas, you might find pipes sold without labels; in that case, measure the inside diameter (ID) as well, because the wall thickness affects flow. For example, a 20mm pipe with thick walls might have an ID of only 15mm, reducing water pressure. Always buy pipes from a reputable supplier who stores them out of direct sunlight, as UV light makes PVC brittle. When cutting, use a hacksaw and then deburr the edges so fittings slide on easily. Remember: the size number on the pipe refers to the outside diameter, not the inside. So a 110mm pipe will not fit into a 110mm fitting if the fitting is meant for a different standard. Always test-fit before gluing.

lessons.title: Understanding the Difference Between PVC, uPVC, and CPVC for Hot and Cold Water
lessons.body: PVC, uPVC, and CPVC are all types of plastic pipes, but they are made differently and used for different jobs. PVC (polyvinyl chloride) is the general term. It often contains plasticizers that make it flexible. You will see grey or white PVC pipes used for drainage and cold water. uPVC (unplasticized PVC) has no plasticizers, so it is rigid and strong. It is the most common pipe for cold water supply and drainage in African homes. uPVC is usually white or grey and comes in sizes from 20mm to 110mm. It cannot handle hot water; above 60Â°C it softens and can burst. CPVC (chlorinated PVC) is PVC that has been chlorinated, making it resistant to higher temperatures. CPVC can handle water up to 90Â°C, so it is used for hot water lines from geysers or solar heaters. CPVC is usually cream or light yellow and is more expensive. In many African markets, CPVC is less common and may need to be ordered. For cold water, always use uPVC. For hot water, use CPVC or PPR (another plastic). Never use ordinary PVC for hot water. If you are unsure, check the pipe marking: it will say 'uPVC' or 'CPVC' and may show a temperature rating. Also, solvent cement for uPVC is different from CPVC cement. You must use the correct cement. For example, uPVC cement will not properly bond CPVC. When buying, ask the supplier for the right cement. In rural areas, you might find only uPVC. For hot water, you can use copper or PPR if available. But for most cold water plumbing, uPVC is your best choice. It is cheap, easy to cut, and lasts for decades if installed correctly. Remember: uPVC and PVC are often used interchangeably in shops, but uPVC is the rigid type you want for plumbing. CPVC is for hot water only. Always read the label.

lessons.title: Tools You Need to Start: Hacksaw, Measuring Tape, and Deburring Tool
lessons.body: To start working with PVC pipes, you need a few basic tools. The most important are a hacksaw, a measuring tape, and a deburring tool. A hacksaw with a fine-tooth blade (24 teeth per inch) is best for cutting PVC. A coarse blade will chip the plastic. You can buy a good hacksaw for about $5 to $10 in most African markets. Always use a mitre box or a steady hand to make straight cuts. A measuring tape, at least 3 meters long, is essential for measuring pipe lengths and marking cut lines. Use a pencil or a permanent marker to mark the pipe. A deburring tool (also called a reamer) removes the burrs inside and outside the pipe after cutting. If you don't have a deburring tool, you can use a pocket knife or sandpaper, but a proper tool is faster and safer. You will also need a solvent cement applicator (a small brush), safety gloves, and safety glasses. For cutting larger pipes (50mm and above), a pipe cutter or a mitre saw can be used, but a hacksaw works fine. When cutting, secure the pipe in a vice or hold it firmly. Cut slowly to avoid cracking. After cutting, deburr both inside and outside. This step is critical: burrs can cause turbulence and leaks. Also, you need a tape measure that locks, so you can measure alone. A small spirit level helps to ensure pipes are straight. For gluing, you need clean rags to wipe dirt. A bucket of water and soap for cleaning hands is also good. In rural areas, you might not find a deburring tool, so use a file or sandpaper. But invest in one if you can; it costs about $3. Always keep your tools clean and dry. A hacksaw blade will last longer if you don't force it. Replace blades when they become dull. With these tools, you can cut and fit PVC pipes for any home repair. Practice on scrap pieces first. Remember: a straight cut and a clean deburr are the secrets to leak-free joints.

lessons.title: How Water Flows: Gravity vs. Pressure Systems in Rural and Urban Settings
lessons.body: Water flows in two main ways: gravity and pressure. In rural areas, many homes use gravity systems. Water is stored in a tank on a roof or a hill, and it flows down through pipes to taps. The higher the tank, the stronger the flow. For every 1 meter of height, you get about 0.1 bar of pressure. So a tank 5 meters above a tap gives about 0.5 bar, which is enough for a slow flow. Gravity systems are simple and don't need pumps, but pressure is low. You must use larger pipes (e.g., 25mm or 32mm) to reduce friction loss. In urban areas, water comes from a mains supply under pressure, often 2 to 4 bar. This pressure pushes water through pipes to your home. You can use smaller pipes (20mm) for supply lines. But high pressure can cause water hammer and leaks, so you need pressure reducers if it's above 4 bar. In both systems, water always flows from high pressure to low pressure. In gravity systems, the height difference creates pressure. In pressure systems, a pump or the municipal supply creates pressure. When designing a system, you must consider flow rate (liters per minute) and pressure. For a gravity system, use a tank at least 3 meters above the highest tap. For pressure systems, ensure pipes are rated for the pressure (uPVC is usually rated for 6 to 10 bar). Also, avoid sharp bends and use elbows to reduce friction. In rural areas, if you have a borehole, you might need a pump to fill the tank. In urban areas, if the mains pressure is low, you might need a booster pump. Always install a stop valve at the tank and at the main entry. For gravity systems, use a float valve in the tank to prevent overflow. For pressure systems, install a pressure gauge to monitor. Remember: water flow is affected by pipe size, length, and fittings. A 20mm pipe can only carry so much water. If you need more flow, use a larger pipe. Test your system by opening a tap and measuring how long it takes to fill a 10-liter bucket. That gives you flow rate in liters per minute. Adjust as needed.

lessons.title: Safety First: Handling PVC Solvent Cement and Cutting Tools
lessons.body: PVC solvent cement is a dangerous chemical. It contains solvents like tetrahydrofuran (THF) and cyclohexanone, which are flammable and toxic. Always work in a well-ventilated area, preferably outdoors or with open windows and fans. Never use it near an open flame or a water heater. Wear safety glasses and chemical-resistant gloves (nitrile or neoprene). Avoid breathing the fumes; if you feel dizzy, move to fresh air immediately. Keep the cement container closed when not in use. Do not smoke while working. Solvent cement can burn your skin, so wash it off with soap and water if you get it on you. If it gets in your eyes, flush with water for 15 minutes and seek medical help. When cutting pipes with a hacksaw, wear safety glasses to protect your eyes from plastic chips. Secure the pipe in a vice or clamp so it doesn't slip. Cut away from your body. Keep your fingers clear of the blade. A dull blade can jump and cut you. After cutting, deburr carefully; the cut edge can be sharp. Use a deburring tool or a file, not your fingers. When using a knife to deburr, cut away from yourself. Store tools safely when not in use. Keep solvent cement out of reach of children. Do not store it in a hot vehicle. The cement has a shelf life; check the date. If it becomes thick or stringy, throw it away. When gluing, work in a well-ventilated space and avoid inhaling deeply. Use a small brush to apply cement, not your fingers. If you spill cement, wipe it up with a rag and dispose of it properly. Do not pour it down the drain. Always have a first aid kit nearby with eye wash and bandages. In rural areas, if you cannot get proper gloves, use thick plastic bags as a temporary barrier, but get proper gloves as soon as possible. Remember: safety is not optional. A few minutes of preparation prevents serious injury.

lessons.title: Local Suppliers: Where to Buy PVC Pipes and Fittings in Your Area
lessons.body: Finding reliable suppliers for PVC pipes and fittings is key to your plumbing work. In most African towns and cities, you can buy from hardware stores, plumbing supply shops, or building material markets. Start by asking local plumbers where they buy their materials. In larger cities, there are specialized plumbing shops that stock a wide range of sizes and fittings. For example, in Nairobi, you can go to Industrial Area; in Lagos, try Ladipo Market; in Accra, go to Kaneshie Market. In rural areas, you might find pipes at general hardware stores or agro-dealers. Always check the quality: look for the manufacturer's mark, the size, and the pressure rating. Avoid pipes that are stored in direct sunlight or that look faded or cracked. When buying, take a sample of the pipe or fitting you need to match. Ask for a discount when buying in bulk. Compare prices at two or three shops. For fittings (elbows, tees, couplings, sockets), ensure they are the same brand and size as the pipe. Mixing brands can cause leaks. If you need CPVC for hot water, you may have to order from a specialized supplier or a larger city. For solvent cement, buy from a reputable shop; cheap cement may not bond properly. Also, consider buying online from platforms like Jumia or Kilimall, but check seller ratings and return policy. For large projects, you can contact manufacturers directly, like Sika, DPI, or local brands. Some suppliers offer delivery for a fee. Build a relationship with your supplier; they can advise you on new products and give you credit. Keep receipts for warranty. In rural areas, you might need to travel to a nearby town to find a good supplier. Plan ahead and buy extra fittings, as they are cheap and you don't want to stop work for a missing elbow. Always inspect pipes before leaving the shop. Check for cracks, warping, or thin walls. A good supplier will let you exchange defective items. Remember: your reputation depends on the quality of your materials. Don't compromise.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: PVC & Plumbing Pipes for African Homes and Small Businesses

This practical reference module gives you the working knowledge to buy, cut, join, and install PVC pipe systems for homes, shops, farms, and small construction jobs. It is written for the African context: metric sizes, local suppliers, and realistic site conditions. Whether you are a plumber, a hardware retailer, or a young entrepreneur starting a plumbing services business, this is your field guide.

PVC (polyvinyl chloride) pipe is the most common plastic pipe in African plumbing because it is cheap, widely available, resistant to corrosion, and easy to work with using simple hand tools. But it is not a "one pipe fits all" material. Hot water, pressure, and chemical exposure all change which pipe you should buy. Getting this wrong costs money and creates callbacks.

1. Common PVC Pipe Sizes in African Homes (20mm to 110mm)

In most of Africa, plumbing pipe is sold by outside diameter (OD) in millimetres, following ISO 1452 and EN 1452 sizing. The sizes you will see on the shelf in Nairobi, Lagos, Accra, Kampala, or Johannesburg are typically 20mm, 25mm, 32mm, 40mm, 50mm, 63mm, 75mm, 90mm, and 110mm. Each size has a job.

Table 1: Typical PVC pipe sizes and common uses in African homes
Nominal Size (OD) Common Use Typical Pressure Class Notes
20mmBasin, sink, and toilet supply linesPN6 to PN10Small, easy to bend around corners
25mmSingle tap or shower supplyPN6 to PN10Good for low-flow rural systems
32mmMain supply to a small housePN6 to PN10Common in gravity systems
40mmMain supply, small garden irrigationPN6 to PN10Balances cost and flow
50mmHouse main, drainage, small farm linesPN6 to PN10Very common on shop shelves
63mmCompound main, small pump linesPN6 to PN10Good for pressure systems
75mmMulti-house supply, drainagePN4 to PN10Check wall thickness
90mmDrainage, sewer, large supply mainsPN4 to PN6Often sold as soil pipe
110mmSoil, waste, sewer, storm drainagePN4 to PN6Standard toilet drain size

Source: Adapted from ISO 1452-2 (PVC-U pipes for water supply) and EN 1452 dimensional tables, as used by major African pipe manufacturers such as SAPPI/Duraplast and Flo-Tek.

2. PVC, uPVC, and CPVC: What Is the Difference?

This is where many installers lose money. The three names sound similar but behave differently:

  • PVC is the general family name. In plumbing shops it often means PVC-U (unplasticised) pipe for cold water and drainage.
  • uPVC (unplasticised PVC) is rigid, strong, and the standard for cold water supply and drainage. It should not be used for hot water above about 40Â°C.
  • CPVC (chlorinated PVC) is PVC that has been chlorinated to raise its temperature tolerance. It handles hot water up to about 90â95Â°C and is used for hot water lines, solar systems, and some industrial work.
Table 2: PVC vs uPVC vs CPVC comparison
Property PVC / uPVC CPVC
Max water temperature~40Â°C (cold water only)~90â95Â°C (hot water)
Pressure ratingPN6âPN16PN10âPN25
CostLow2â4Ã more expensive
Sunlight resistancePoor (needs paint or shade)Better, but still fades
Common useCold supply, drainage, irrigationHot water, solar, industrial
Solvent cementPVC cementCPVC-specific cement only

Source: Adapted from ASTM D1785 / D2846 and Lubrizol CPVC technical data, widely cited by African plumbing suppliers.

Business tip: Stock both uPVC and CPVC if you serve hotels, clinics, or solar water heating customers. A single hot-water job can pay more than ten cold-water repairs.

3. Tools You Need to Start

You do not need a big workshop. A basic PVC kit fits in a bucket:

  • Hacksaw with a fine-tooth blade (24 TPI) for clean square cuts.
  • Measuring tape (5m minimum) and a pencil or marker.
  • Deburring tool or half-round file to remove the inner and outer burr after cutting.
  • Pipe cutter (optional, faster for 20â40mm).
  • Solvent cement and applicator brush.
  • Clean rag and primer if required locally.
  • Spirit level and string line for straight runs.
  • Safety glasses and gloves.

4. How Water Flows: Gravity vs Pressure

Understanding flow decides the pipe size and pressure class you buy.

  • Gravity systems rely on height. A tank 5m above a tap gives roughly 0.5 bar. Use larger pipes (32mmâ50mm) to reduce friction loss. Common in rural homes and smallholder farms.
  • Pressure systems use a pump (booster, submersible, or jet pump). They can push water long distances and uphill. Use pressure-rated pipe (PN10 or higher) and check joints carefully.
  • Rule of thumb: every 10m of height gives about 1 bar; every 10m of pipe adds friction loss. Undersized pipe kills pressure.
â  SAFETY WARNING â PVC Solvent Cement and Cutting Tools

PVC solvent cement is flammable, toxic, and gives off strong fumes. Work outdoors or in a well-ventilated area. Keep away from open flames, cigarettes, and sparks. Wear nitrile gloves and safety glasses. Do not breathe the vapour. Store cement in a cool, locked place away from children. When using a hacksaw, clamp the pipe securely and cut away from your body. Never cut toward your hand. Dispose of cement rags and shavings safely â they can ignite.

5. Local Suppliers: Where to Buy

Buying smart is a business skill. In most African cities you will find PVC pipe at:

  • Hardware shops and building material yards in industrial areas.
  • Specialist plumbing merchants (often near main markets or industrial parks).
  • Manufacturer depots (e.g., Duraplast, Flo-Tek, SAPPI, Plasco, and regional brands).
  • Online marketplaces such as Jumia, Kilimall, or local construction apps for small orders.

Buying tips: Always check the pressure class printed on the pipe (PN6, PN10, PN16). Ask for the manufacturer's certificate. Buy fittings from the same brand where possible â sizes vary slightly between makers. Negotiate bulk prices; a 10% discount on a 100-pipe order is real profit.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Measure the run and choose the correct pipe size (20mm for taps, 110mm for soil).
  2. Confirm cold (uPVC) or hot (CPVC) service before buying.
  3. Check the pressure class (PN6 minimum; PN10 for pressure systems).
  4. Cut square with a fine-tooth hacksaw and deburr both ends.
  5. Dry-fit all joints before applying solvent cement.
  6. Apply cement evenly, twist a quarter turn, and hold for 30 seconds.
  7. Allow 24 hours curing before pressure testing.
  8. Store cement and tools safely, away from children and flames.

Further Reading (Free Official Sources)

  • ISO 1452-2 â PVC-U pipes for water supply (ISO)
  • WHO Guidelines for Drinking-water Quality (WHO)
  • Practical Action Technical Briefs â Water and Sanitation
  • UNICEF WASH Programme Resources
  • ASTM D1785 â Standard Specification for PVC Plastic Pipe

Business takeaway: PVC plumbing is a repeat business. Homes leak, farms expand, and hotels upgrade. Master pipe sizing, material selection, and safe solvent welding, and you can quote confidently, reduce callbacks, and build a profitable plumbing or supply business anywhere in Africa.

quiz.q: What does the size number on a PVC pipe (e.g., 110mm) refer to?
quiz.explanation: The size number on PVC pipes indicates the outside diameter, which is standard for fittings.

quiz.q: Which PVC pipe size is commonly used for underground sewer lines?
quiz.explanation: 110mm pipes are the standard for underground sewer and toilet outlets.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid buying PVC pipes stored in direct sunlight?
options: A) They become too hot to handle
B) UV light makes them brittle
quiz.explanation: UV light degrades PVC, making it brittle and prone to cracking.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between PVC and uPVC?
options: A) uPVC is flexible, PVC is rigid
B) uPVC has no plasticizers, PVC has plasticizers
C) uPVC is for hot water, PVC for cold
D) uPVC is blue, PVC is white
quiz.explanation: uPVC is unplasticized, meaning it lacks plasticizers, making it rigid and strong.

quiz.q: Which type of pipe is suitable for hot water up to 90Â°C?
quiz.explanation: CPVC is chlorinated PVC and can handle hot water up to 90Â°C.

quiz.q: What happens if you use ordinary PVC for hot water?
options: B) It softens and can burst
quiz.explanation: Ordinary PVC softens above 60Â°C and can burst under pressure.

quiz.q: Which cement should you use for CPVC pipes?
quiz.explanation: CPVC requires special CPVC cement; uPVC cement will not bond properly.

quiz.q: What is the best blade for cutting PVC with a hacksaw?
quiz.explanation: A fine-tooth blade (24 TPI) cuts PVC cleanly without chipping.

quiz.q: Why is deburring important after cutting PVC pipe?
options: A) It makes the pipe look nice
B) It removes burrs that cause turbulence and leaks
D) It helps glue dry faster
quiz.explanation: Deburring removes rough edges that can disrupt flow and prevent proper fitting.

quiz.q: What can you use if you don't have a deburring tool?
options: B) A pocket knife or sandpaper
quiz.explanation: A pocket knife or sandpaper can be used to remove burrs if a deburring tool is unavailable.

quiz.q: How much pressure does 1 meter of water height create in a gravity system?
quiz.explanation: Every 1 meter of height gives about 0.1 bar of pressure.

quiz.q: In a gravity system, what is the minimum recommended height of the tank above the highest tap?
quiz.explanation: A minimum of 3 meters height ensures adequate flow for most taps.

quiz.q: What is a common pressure range for urban mains water supply?
quiz.explanation: Urban mains pressure is typically between 2 and 4 bar.

quiz.q: Why might you need a pressure reducer in an urban setting?
options: B) To prevent water hammer and leaks
quiz.explanation: High pressure above 4 bar can cause water hammer and damage pipes, so a reducer is used.

quiz.q: What is the main hazard of PVC solvent cement?
options: A) It is flammable and toxic
B) It is corrosive to metal
quiz.explanation: Solvent cement contains flammable and toxic solvents like THF.

quiz.q: What should you do if you get solvent cement in your eyes?
options: B) Flush with water for 15 minutes and seek medical help
D) Close your eyes and rest
quiz.explanation: Immediate flushing with water for 15 minutes is necessary, followed by medical attention.

quiz.q: Why should you work in a well-ventilated area when using solvent cement?
options: A) To avoid dizziness from fumes
B) To make glue dry faster
C) To keep the pipe cool
quiz.explanation: Solvent fumes can cause dizziness and are harmful if inhaled.

quiz.q: What type of gloves are recommended when handling solvent cement?
quiz.explanation: Chemical-resistant gloves like nitrile or neoprene protect skin from solvents.

quiz.q: What should you do with a hacksaw when not in use?
options: A) Leave it on the floor
B) Store it safely with blade covered
C) Hang it on a nail
D) Put it in your pocket
quiz.explanation: Store tools safely to prevent accidents, ideally with blade guard or in a toolbox.

quiz.q: Why is it important to secure the pipe in a vice when cutting?
options: B) To prevent slipping and injury
C) To keep the pipe straight
quiz.explanation: Securing the pipe prevents it from slipping, reducing the risk of cuts.

quiz.q: Where can you often find a wide range of PVC pipes and fittings in a city?
options: B) Plumbing supply shops or building material markets
quiz.explanation: Specialized plumbing shops and building markets stock a variety of sizes and fittings.

quiz.q: What should you check on a PVC pipe before buying?
options: B) Manufacturer's mark, size, and pressure rating
quiz.explanation: These markings ensure you get the correct and quality pipe.

quiz.q: Why is it recommended to buy fittings from the same brand as the pipe?
options: B) They match in size and ensure proper fit
quiz.explanation: Mixing brands can lead to size mismatches and leaks.

quiz.q: What advantage does building a relationship with your supplier give?
quiz.explanation: A good relationship can lead to helpful advice and credit terms.

quiz.q: What should you do if you find a defective pipe at the shop?
options: D) Use it for a different purpose
quiz.explanation: Defective pipes should be exchanged to ensure quality work.

quiz.q: Which of these is a common online platform to buy plumbing supplies in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Jumia is a popular African e-commerce platform that sells plumbing supplies.

quiz.q: What is the recommended minimum pipe size for a gravity-fed supply line to a tap?
quiz.explanation: 25mm is often recommended for gravity systems to reduce friction loss.

quiz.q: What does a pressure rating of 6 bar on a uPVC pipe mean?
options: A) It can handle up to 6 bar pressure
quiz.explanation: The pressure rating indicates the maximum pressure the pipe can safely handle.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid sharp bends in a pipe system?
options: B) They increase friction and reduce flow
C) They are hard to install
quiz.explanation: Sharp bends cause turbulence and pressure loss, so elbows are used instead.

quiz.q: What is a simple way to test the flow rate of your system?
options: A) Measure how long to fill a 10-liter bucket
quiz.explanation: Timing how long it takes to fill a known volume gives flow rate in liters per minute.
